en.title: Lee Chang-dong Returns: 'Possible Love' Explores Filmmaking Ethics and Class Divide
en.summary: After an eight-year hiatus, the acclaimed director **Lee Chang-dong** is back with his most intricate film yet, **Possible Love**. Inspired by Krzysztof Kieslowski's 'Dekalog,' the movie tackles labor rights, class struggles, and the moral complexities of capturing real lives on screen.
en.body:
The masterful **Lee Chang-dong**, a filmmaker known for his patient yet piercing portraits of ordinary people pushed to their limits, has finally returned. After an eight-year wait since the critically acclaimed **Burning**, Lee's seventh feature, **Possible Love**, premiered at the Venice Film Festival, earning the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize. This expansive, nearly three-hour drama draws inspiration from Krzysztof Kieslowski's **Dekalog**, specifically the tenth commandment, 'Thou Shall Not Covet,' but Lee masterfully transforms this into a complex character study on the imbalanced dynamics of human connection, labor, and filmmaking ethics.

**Possible Love** centers on two couples separated by a stark class divide, brought together by the creation of a documentary. We meet **Ho-seok** (played by **Sul Kyung-gu**), a factory worker whose life is upended by brutal layoffs following a labor strike—a story loosely based on the real-life 2009 Ssangyong Motor incident. His wife, **Mi-ok** (**Jeon Do-yeon**), struggles to maintain their family in the difficult aftermath. Their lives intersect with **Ye-ji** (**Cho Yeo-jeong**), a filmmaker documenting the injustices of the labor movement, and her affluent husband, **Sang-woo** (**Zo In-sung**). Ye-ji sees Ho-seok as the ideal subject for her film, and as the documentary project unfolds, the lines between observer and observed begin to blur, exposing suppressed feelings, professional ambitions, and hidden desires.

## The Camera's Gaze and Moral Mazes

Lee Chang-dong himself acknowledges that the film grapples with questions he asks of himself as a storyteller. The narrative delves into the ethical considerations inherent in portraying vulnerable individuals and their struggles. It's a slow-burn examination, not of mortal peril, but of moral quandaries, forcing viewers to confront the power dynamics at play when one person's life becomes another's narrative. The film is a testament to Lee's signature style: intricate, deeply human, and unafraid to explore the uncomfortable truths that lie beneath the surface of everyday life.

## A Masterclass in Character and Consequence

Fans of **Lee Chang-dong** have eagerly awaited his return, and **Possible Love** delivers a haunting, masterful experience. The film's critical success at Venice, including the FIPRESCI prize, underscores its impact. For cinephiles, it's a profound meditation on empathy, exploitation, and the very nature of storytelling. The film's exploration of class division and the ethics of documentary filmmaking is particularly relevant today, sparking conversations about representation and the responsibilities of creators. It’s a film that lingers long after the credits roll, prompting introspection on our own roles and perspectives.

## What's Next

**Possible Love** was South Korea's official selection for International Feature Film at the 2027 Academy Awards. The film is now available on Netflix, allowing audiences worldwide to experience **Lee Chang-dong**'s latest compelling work.

content_raw: Lee Chang-dong has never been in a hurry. The novelist-turned-filmmaker (and one-time South Korean minister of culture) has made just seven features in nearly thirty years; Peppermint Candy , Secret Sunshine , and Burning among the most celebrated, each a patient, piercing portrait of ordinary people pushed to the edge. Needless to say, the eight years since Burning have felt like a long time to wait for another. Now, Lee is back with Possible Love , featuring an immersive quartet of characters and an ethical puzzle only he could jigsaw together so effectively. The film premiered in Venice in September, where it won the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize (and FIPRESCI Prize) 24 years after Oasis earned Lee the Silver Lion for Best Director. The setup is simple: two couples on opposite sides of a class divide, brought together by the making of a documentary. Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu) is a factory worker who was laid off after a labor strike came to a brutal end, the story loosely based on the 2009 Ssangyong Motor layoffs. Meanwhile, his wife, Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), tries to hold their family together in the aftermath. At a funeral, they meet Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a filmmaker making a documentary about the injustices of the labor movement, and her wealthy husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). Of course, Ye-ji sees Ho-seok as the perfect subject, and soon the situation starts to get muddy. Over nearly three hours, the two couples become entangled as suppressed feelings, professional ambitions (or the severe lack thereof), and hidden desires surface. Lee, for his part, makes no secret that these are questions he’s asking of himself, too. On the heels of the film’s Netflix release, we sat down with the acclaimed writer-director to talk about the ethics of the camera’s gaze, the subject’s relationship to the storyteller, and the potential for union and solidarity between art and labor. The Film Stage: I want to start by asking you about the role of a filmmaker in a subject’s life, because that’s such a big part of this film. The winding ethics of that situation serve as the dramatic thrust of the film. So what do you think is the role of a documentary filmmaker documenting a subject’s life? Lee Chang-dong : While this film shows a character who’s a documentary filmmaker and tells the story partly about the attitude, the ethics, and the distance between the documentary filmmaker and her subject, it’s also a question that I want to raise through the story. Documentary filmmakers, more so than feature filmmakers, are more sensitive to this line of ethics, I think. And that’s because they are closer to the subject that they’re portraying. You know, depending on what kind of person they’re portraying, what kind of pain they’re capturing, how deep the wounds are, and the other elements at play.
